parole.testo: From Old Swedish armborst, from Middle Low German armborst, from Medieval Latin arcuballista, arbalista, from arcus + ballista. First attested in the early 14th century. Compare Danish and Norwegian armbrøst, German Armbrust, English arbalest.
From Old Swedish blidha, borrowed (likely through Middle Low German blîde) from Medieval Latin blida. Ultimately from Ancient Greek βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German burs, buss (“comrade; boy”), further from Medieval Latin bursa (“purse”). Attested since 1697.

parole.significato: gun (shooting weapon functioning through stored energy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish byssa, bössa (“rifle, cannon, box”), from Middle Low German büsse (“box, gun”), from Medieval Latin buxis, from Ancient Greek πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s), from πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos, “box wood”). Doublet of bussa (“to fit with a bushing”). Cognate with bush.
From Middle Low German karpe, from Medieval Latin carpa, of Germanic, but ultimately non-Indo-European origin; see Old High German karpho.

parole.significato: receipt (written acknowledgement of payment, delivery, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvittancia, from Middle Low German quitancie, from Medieval Latin quitantia, from Latin quietantia. Cognate of English quittance, German Quittanz, French quittance, Italian quietanza.

Inherited from Old Swedish sedel, borrowed from Middle Low German sēdel, sēdele, sēdule, derived from Medieval Latin cedula, from earlier Latin schedula. Cognate to Danish seddel, Norwegian seddel, Icelandic seðill, German Zettel, French cédule, English schedule, Hungarian cédula.

parole.significato: sand lance (fish of the family Ammodytidae)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tobies, from Medieval Latin Tobīās.
